headline: Have the Brussels Region formally recognise gynaecological and obstetric violence and require official data-gathering, training for health staff, patient information, and a clear route to lodge complaints.
title: La proposition vise à faire reconnaître par la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale les violences gynécologiques et obstétricales et à mettre en place la collecte de données, la sensibilisation du personnel soignant, l'information des patientes et un dispositif de plainte. Des amendements ajoutent la mise à disposition et le financement d'interprètes en langue des signes pour les femmes sourdes ainsi que des outils d'information accessibles.
raw_outcome: La proposition vise à faire reconnaître par la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale les violences gynécologiques et obstétricales et à mettre en place la collecte de données, la sensibilisation du personnel soignant, l'information des patientes et un dispositif de plainte. Des amendements ajoutent la mise à disposition et le financement d'interprètes en langue des signes pour les femmes sourdes ainsi que des outils d'information accessibles.
source_brief:
Belgium keeps no official national figures on gynaecological and obstetric violence — no public database, no structured reporting system — so the scale is known only from citizen surveys. This resolution would have the Brussels Region put a name to the problem and act on it: collect data, train health staff, inform patients of their rights, and open a clear path to complain. It covers acts such as examinations or procedures done without consent or explanation, pressure during labour, and the so-called "husband stitch". Late additions ask hospitals to provide sign-language interpreters for deaf women and to fund that interpretation so cost is no barrier.

- **What it asks for** — formal recognition by the Region, a data-collection mechanism, staff training, patient-rights information, and an accessible complaints route.
- **Why now** — a citizen-platform survey put a number on something the official statistics ignore, and a Senate report flagged the missing consolidated data.
- **Disability angle** — added asks oblige health establishments to supply French- and Flemish-sign-language interpreters across prenatal, birth and postnatal care, financed so it doesn't fall on the patient.
- **The rub:** supporters say a region that names the problem and counts it can finally tackle it; opponents argue maternal care and hospital norms sit largely with the federal and Community levels, so a Brussels resolution adds paperwork to already-stretched medical staff without real power to act.
deep_facts:
- The resolution concerns gynaecological and obstetric violence: acts experienced as abusive or non-consented during gynaecological care, childbirth and perinatal care, including procedures without effective anaesthesia, abdominal (fundal) pressure, episiotomy, and the "husband stitch" (CRI, 6 Feb 2026; doc A-29).
- Stated context: Belgium has no specific official national statistics on these violences, no public database and no structured reporting system; the Senate report flags missing consolidated figures and data-collection mechanisms (CRI, 6 Feb 2026).
- Cited survey figures (estimated, from a citizen platform for respected birth / "naissance respectée"): one woman in five reports such violence during childbirth or perinatal care; one woman in three among racialised women (CRI, 6 Feb 2026).
- A second 2021 study cited yields a figure of two women in five when verbal, physical and psychological violence are added to the "à vif" acts, abdominal pressure and husband stitch (CRI, 6 Feb 2026).
- The operative text (text adopted by the commission) seeks, as its first request, recognition of these violences by the Brussels-Capital Region, plus data collection, staff training/awareness, patient information and a complaints route (CRI, 6 Feb 2026; doc A-29).
- Two amendments tabled in plenary (am. 1, two new tirets; am. 2, one new tiret) add: requiring health establishments to make available French Belgian (LSFB) and Flemish (VGT) sign-language interpreters at all contacts with deaf women — notably prenatal consultations, delivery and postnatal follow-up — via complementary non-organic hospital norms; financing sign-language interpretation so its cost is not a barrier to gynaecological/obstetric care; and promoting accessible information and awareness tools in sign language on patients' rights, forms of violence and available support, plus improved staff training on disability specifics (CRI, 6 Feb 2026; am. 1 and am. 2, A-29).
- Levels-of-power references: a federal interfederal working group on follow-up of professional recommendations was foreseen under the National Action Plan against gender-based violence 2021–2025, supervised by the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men, with the federated entities represented; the proposers also cite a parallel training proposal lodged in the Federation Wallonia-Brussels based on Senate recommendations (CRI, 6 Feb 2026).
deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- **What it enables:** a regional act of naming plus a data mandate — once a phenomenon is officially counted, it becomes governable (budgets, norms, follow-up questions). The first ask, "recognition," is the lever: it converts a contested experience into an administrative fact the Region must then track.
- **Second-order effects:** the sign-language amendments quietly create a financing obligation ("interpretation cost is not a barrier") and reach into hospital norms — a concrete, costed lever bolted onto an otherwise declaratory text.
- **The wedge:** the competence question. Much of maternal care and hospital norms is federal/Community, so the fight is less about whether the violence exists than about whether a Brussels resolution is the right instrument or symbolic overreach that loads administration onto clinicians. The proposers pre-empt this by stressing "normes hospitalières" the Region can touch and the precedent of guaranteeing IVG access in Brussels hospitals.
proposed_by: Ecolo, PS, PTB, DéFI (De Ré, Stoops, Tahar, De Smedt, El Yousfi, Cruysmans, Mandaila)

headline: Encourage all nineteen Brussels communes to declare themselves "safe spaces for women" by adopting charters and proactive policies against sexist and sexual violence in local political life.
title: La proposition invite les dix-neuf communes bruxelloises à se déclarer « lieux sûrs pour les femmes » et à lutter contre les violences sexistes et sexuelles dans l'exercice des fonctions politiques locales, en s'inspirant d'une charte adoptée à Schaerbeek. Le plan s'articule autour de six axes : chartes et politiques proactives, formation et sensibilisation, procédures de signalement claires et indépendantes, prévention, suivi démocratique et intégration transversale de la dimension de genre.
raw_outcome: La proposition invite les dix-neuf communes bruxelloises à se déclarer « lieux sûrs pour les femmes » et à lutter contre les violences sexistes et sexuelles dans l'exercice des fonctions politiques locales, en s'inspirant d'une charte adoptée à Schaerbeek. Le plan s'articule autour de six axes : chartes et politiques proactives, formation et sensibilisation, procédures de signalement claires et indépendantes, prévention, suivi démocratique et intégration transversale de la dimension de genre.
source_brief:
Sexist and sexual violence reaches into political life: one survey found 18% of women elected officials had faced sexual harassment during their mandate, and in 2022 more than 120 Belgian women politicians signed an open letter denouncing it inside the institutions. This resolution would push all nineteen Brussels communes to declare themselves "safe spaces for women" — modelled on a charter first adopted in Schaerbeek — and to build out a six-part plan around it. The text is a regional resolution encouraging the communes; it does not bind them.

- **What it does** — invites every commune to adopt a charter and proactive policy, train and raise awareness, set up clear independent reporting procedures, act in prevention, ensure democratic follow-up, and mainstream gender across the plan.
- **Where it comes from** — a charter adopted in Schaerbeek, presented as the first Belgian commune to commit to one, scaled up to the whole Region.
- **The rub:** supporters call it a low-cost way to spread a proven good practice to the level closest to citizens; sceptics note it is a non-binding nudge to communes over their own internal conduct, with the substantive legal protections (Istanbul Convention, the 2023 femicide law) already existing — so the question is whether a regional charter changes behaviour or mainly signals.
deep_facts:
- The resolution invites the nineteen Brussels communes to declare themselves "safe spaces for women" ("lieux sûrs pour les femmes") and to combat sexist and sexual violence in the exercise of local political functions (CRI, 6 Feb 2026; doc A-192).
- It is presented as inspired by a motion adopted unanimously in Schaerbeek, cited as the first Belgian commune to adopt a charter of commitment and actions against sexist and sexual violence in politics; the aim stated is to extend those good practices to all communes (CRI, 6 Feb 2026).
- The plan is articulated around six axes (CRI, 6 Feb 2026): (1) create safe spaces for women by encouraging all communes to adopt charters and proactive policies and to exchange good practices; (2) increase training and awareness; (3) put in place clear, independent and protective reporting procedures; (4) act in prevention; (5) ensure democratic follow-up; (6) mainstream the gender dimension transversally across the plan.
- Cited figures (estimated/surveyed): a 2018 survey found 18% of women elected officials reported sexual harassment during their mandate and 34% outside it; in 2022 more than 120 Belgian women politicians across political families signed an open letter denouncing sexist behaviour and sexual or psychological harassment within the institutions (CRI, 6 Feb 2026).
- Existing legal framework referenced (not created by this text): the Istanbul Convention, a Council of Europe resolution, and the 2023 law on prevention of and combating femicides, gender-based homicides and violence; the proposers state the gap is operational implementation at local level, not the absence of legislation (CRI, 6 Feb 2026).
- Process note: in commission, amendments originating from PS, MR and N-VA were incorporated into the text (CRI, 6 Feb 2026; doc A-192).
deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- **What it enables:** a regional template that communes can adopt off the shelf, lowering the cost of acting and creating peer pressure (a commune that declines a "safe space" charter has to explain why). The instrument is soft — "encourage," not "oblige" — so its bite depends entirely on uptake.
- **Second-order effects:** the "clear, independent reporting procedures" axis is the operative one — it points at internal complaint channels for elected officials and local staff, the part with real institutional consequences; the rest (charters, awareness, mainstreaming) is largely declaratory.
- **The tension:** competence and scope. The proposers concede the legal protections already exist federally/internationally and frame the value as "operationalising" them locally — which is also the line of attack: a non-binding regional resolution about communes' own conduct can be read as signalling rather than change. The cross-party amendment uptake suggests a deliberate consensus play (broad sign-on lowers the cost of voting for it).
proposed_by: Ecolo, PS, DéFI (Tahar, Khattabi, De Ré, Luhahi, Vidal, Agic, Mandaila)

headline: Reform Actiris's jobseeker availability-check procedure: abolish the three-evaluator college, check 100% of jobseekers' availability (instead of today's partial coverage), and extend from two to four months the deadline for Actiris to offer training, an internship or a job.
title: La proposition vise à réformer la procédure de contrôle de la disponibilité des chercheurs d'emploi à Actiris : supprimer le collège d'évaluation composé de trois évaluateurs, réaffecter le personnel ainsi libéré, atteindre un taux de couverture de 100 % des chercheurs d'emploi et contrôler leur disponibilité deux fois (à l'analyse du dossier puis, en cas d'évaluation négative, lors d'un entretien). Le texte prévoit un plan d'action individuel dans les 30 jours et porte de deux à quatre mois le délai dans lequel Actiris doit proposer une formation, un stage d'insertion ou une offre d'emploi. Le texte soumis au vote a été amendé en séance, des amendements concurrents en modifiant la portée.
raw_outcome: La proposition vise à réformer la procédure de contrôle de la disponibilité des chercheurs d'emploi à Actiris : supprimer le collège d'évaluation composé de trois évaluateurs, réaffecter le personnel ainsi libéré, atteindre un taux de couverture de 100 % des chercheurs d'emploi et contrôler leur disponibilité deux fois (à l'analyse du dossier puis, en cas d'évaluation négative, lors d'un entretien). Le texte prévoit un plan d'action individuel dans les 30 jours et porte de deux à quatre mois le délai dans lequel Actiris doit proposer une formation, un stage d'insertion ou une offre d'emploi. Le texte soumis au vote a été amendé en séance, des amendements concurrents en modifiant la portée.
source_brief:
Today only about 20% of Brussels jobseekers get an accompaniment, and a college of three evaluators sits in the availability-control chain. This resolution reworks that procedure at Actiris: scrap the three-evaluator college, redeploy those staff to counselling, and aim to check the availability of 100% of jobseekers — once when the file is analysed, and again in an interview if that first check is negative. It also stretches from two to four months the window in which Actiris must offer training, an internship or a job, and sets a 30-day target for an individual action plan. The text put to the vote was reworked in session, with competing amendments pulling it in different directions.

- **What changes** — the evaluator college goes; freed-up staff move to counselling; availability is checked for everyone, twice if needed; the offer deadline goes from two to four months; an individual action plan within 30 days.
- **The numbers behind it** — ~92,000 jobseekers, ~21,000 vacancies in the Actiris database; ten jobseekers for every available low-skilled job; Brussels unemployment 21.2% (2014) to 15.4% (2025).
- **The fight over the amendments** — one bloc frames the redeployed staff as straight "control" of availability; a competing bloc would instead fold availability assessment into a capabilities-based accompaniment, bar any unfavourable decision without a real, adapted job-offer first, and build in procedural safeguards and appeals.
- **The rub:** is checking everyone's availability a fairer "nudge" that frees staff to actually help — or does tightening control do little when there aren't enough jobs (ten seekers per low-skilled post), risking sanctions and transfers to the CPAS without creating work?
deep_facts:
- The resolution reforms the procedure for controlling jobseekers' availability at Actiris (CRI, 6 Feb 2026; doc A-145). It was discussed jointly with related texts A-162, A-165 and A-168.
- Core operative asks (as argued by the proposers and reflected in the cosigned amendments n° 1–4): abolish the college of three evaluators; redeploy the freed human resources to jobseeker evaluation/counselling; reach a coverage target of 100% of jobseekers; check availability twice — first at file analysis and, if the assessment is negative ("suite à l'analyse sur dossier"), a second time in an interview; an individual action plan within 30 days; and, by amending the seventh tiret, replace "two" with "four" months as the deadline within which Actiris must propose a training, an insertion internship or a job offer — aligning Brussels with the Walloon Region (CRI, 6 Feb 2026; am. n° 1, 2, 3, 4, A-145).
- Amendment n° 3 also changes the competence-balance (bilan de compétences) wording and replaces the figure "15" with "30" (days) for the individual action plan (CRI, 6 Feb 2026; am. n° 3).
- A competing set of amendments (n° 5–17, tabled by Tahar/Laanan and, for several, Luhahi) would instead: integrate active-availability assessment into the accompaniment process via a common methodology validated by Actiris's management committee, based on a "capabilities" approach; redeploy agents from active-availability control to employment-counsellor roles while keeping a specialised passive-availability service (about 8 FTE) and the dispensations cell; set up a methodological-support mechanism of referents (including former evaluators) to ensure consistency and validate signalements before transmission to passive availability; bar any unfavourable active-availability decision without a real, adapted, duly-notified accompaniment offer; add procedural safeguards (motivation in fact and law, reasonable deadlines, accessible information, right to assistance, effective internal appeals); ensure continuity for jobseekers reaching end-of-rights in liaison with the CPAS; and extend an evaluation reporting period from one year to two with named indicators (CRI, 6 Feb 2026; am. n° 5–17, A-145).
- Cited figures: about 92,000 jobseekers and 21,000 job offers in the Actiris database; a BECI study reports 100,000 vacancies; roughly ten jobseekers per available low-skilled job; only about 20% of jobseekers currently benefit from accompaniment under the current procedure (CRI, 6 Feb 2026).
- Cited labour-market figures (stated): Brussels employment rate 54% (2014) rising to 64% (2025); unemployment rate 21.2% (2014) falling to 15.4% (2025); comparison cities — Antwerp 14.9%, Liège 23.3%, Charleroi 22.8%; youth unemployment cited at about 25% (CRI, 6 Feb 2026).
- Procedural references: the current availability-control device is organised by the arrêté of 16 February 2017; the proposers cite a recent Brupartners opinion and federal measures pushing a more demanding follow-up; the competing bloc references articles 51 to 53bis of the royal decree of 25 November 1991 for passive-availability handling (CRI, 6 Feb 2026).
deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- **What it enables:** removing the evaluator college and pushing toward 100% coverage reframes availability control from a specialised gatekeeping body into a routine, universal check folded into counselling — which can be read as "more help" (more agents counselling) or "more control" (everyone screened), and the text is deliberately ambiguous between the two.
- **The wedge that defines the vote:** two rival visions sit on the same skeleton. One bloc keeps the language of control (check whether you found a job / attended an interview) and budget-neutral redeployment; the rival bloc rewires the same machinery toward a capabilities approach, makes any unfavourable decision conditional on a genuine prior offer, and adds appeals and safeguards. A voter's instinct on "control vs. support" is the real fault line, not the abolition of the college, which both broadly accept.
- **Second-order effects:** stretching the offer deadline from two to four months loosens the timer in the jobseeker's favour but also delays the point at which a negative assessment can bite; the "no unfavourable decision without a real offer" amendment, if it lands, shifts the burden onto Actiris to have delivered first — a structurally different regime from a pure coverage target.
- **Tension:** the macro argument (ten seekers per low-skilled job; ~92,000 seekers vs ~21,000 listed vacancies) cuts against the premise that tighter checking yields more hires — raising whether the reform mainly accelerates transfers to the CPAS rather than to work.
proposed_by: DéFI, Anders (de Patoul, Belguenani); in-session amendments from MR and CD&V, with competing amendments from PS and Ecolo

headline: Have the Brussels Parliament call on the federal government to condemn the Iranian regime's repression, support the Iranian people's aspirations, protect dissidents and journalists, and break off diplomatic normalisation with the Islamic Republic of Iran.
title: La proposition demande au gouvernement fédéral et au ministre des Affaires étrangères de condamner les exactions du régime théocratique autoritaire iranien, de soutenir les aspirations légitimes du peuple iranien à la liberté et à l'autodétermination, de soutenir le droit à la communication et la levée du blocus numérique, de garantir une protection internationale renforcée aux dissidents, journalistes, avocats et activistes, et de rompre toute normalisation diplomatique avec la République islamique d'Iran. Des amendements ajoutent un appel à éviter l'escalade militaire et l'expression de la solidarité avec la population iranienne.
raw_outcome: La proposition demande au gouvernement fédéral et au ministre des Affaires étrangères de condamner les exactions du régime théocratique autoritaire iranien, de soutenir les aspirations légitimes du peuple iranien à la liberté et à l'autodétermination, de soutenir le droit à la communication et la levée du blocus numérique, de garantir une protection internationale renforcée aux dissidents, journalistes, avocats et activistes, et de rompre toute normalisation diplomatique avec la République islamique d'Iran. Des amendements ajoutent un appel à éviter l'escalade militaire et l'expression de la solidarité avec la population iranienne.
source_brief:
Since 28 December 2025, Iran has violently repressed mass peaceful protests that grew out of an economic crisis into a challenge to the regime. This resolution has the Brussels Parliament address the federal government and the foreign-affairs minister: condemn the theocratic regime's abuses, back the Iranian people's aspirations to freedom and self-determination, support the right to information and lifting the digital blackout, guarantee reinforced international protection for dissidents, journalists, lawyers and binational activists, and end diplomatic normalisation with Iran. It is a position statement, addressed to the federal level, on a matter where the Region's international powers are limited.

- **What it asks** — federal condemnation of the regime, support for the protesters' aspirations and for communication rights, protection for dissidents and journalists, and a break in diplomatic normalisation.
- **Where it points** — to the federal government and foreign-affairs minister; it cites the EU Council's 29 January 2026 listing of the Revolutionary Guards as a terrorist organisation and a European Parliament resolution of 22 January 2026.
- **The rub:** is a regional parliament right to take a clear, hard line (condemn, protect, break ties) on an international crisis where Brussels has real symbolic weight — or do automatic sanctions and a diplomatic rupture risk adding to the population's suffering, the line that drives the debate over softer, dialogue-first wording?
deep_facts:
- The resolution asks the federal government (and the minister of foreign affairs) to: condemn the abuses of Iran's authoritarian theocratic regime against its population; support the Iranian people's legitimate aspirations to freedom of expression and to democratically decide their future; support the right to communication and information and favour lifting the digital blackout; guarantee reinforced international protection to dissidents, journalists, lawyers and binational activists; and break off diplomatic normalisation with the Islamic Republic of Iran, preventing the regime from harming Belgium and the EU by all legal, diplomatic and financial means (CRI, 6 Feb 2026; doc A-236).
- Trigger stated: the repression of peaceful protests since 28 December 2025, which began amid an economic crisis (collapse of the rial) and turned into contestation of the theocratic regime; the regime has been in place since 1979 (cited as 47 years) (CRI, 6 Feb 2026).
- Cited figures (stated in debate, attributed to speakers): a population of about 90–92 million; claims of "more than 30,000" dead and of executions "in the tens of thousands" (figures presented as not yet precisely established); particularly intense repression cited on 8, 9 and 10 January; a cited STEM female-graduate rate approaching 70% (CRI, 6 Feb 2026).
- External decisions referenced (not enacted by this text): the European Council decision of 29 January 2026 listing the Revolutionary Guards as a terrorist organisation; a European Parliament resolution of 22 January 2026 on the repression; condemnations by UN bodies including the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (CRI, 6 Feb 2026).
- The base text put to the vote (text adopted by the commission) comprised considerants 1 to 21 and points 1 to 4 of the dispositif (CRI, 6 Feb 2026; doc A-236).
- Two amendments tabled in plenary (am. n° 1 and n° 2, by Parga Vega) would add: a new point calling on all parties to the conflict to avoid military escalation and seek a peaceful solution through diplomatic dialogue in respect of international law; and a new point expressing solidarity with the Iranian population suffering from the economic crisis, political repression, executions and arbitrary state violence, as well as from international sanctions and geopolitical tensions (CRI, 6 Feb 2026; am. n° 1 and n° 2, A-236).
- Competence note stated: the Brussels-Capital Region has international powers limited to its areas of autonomy; the proposers stress Brussels as host to EU and NATO institutions (CRI, 6 Feb 2026).
deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- **What it enables:** a sub-national parliament adding its voice to a federal/EU foreign-policy track it cannot itself execute — the asks are addressed upward (to the federal government and foreign minister), so the resolution's force is symbolic and agenda-setting, leveraging Brussels' status as a diplomatic capital.
- **The wedge:** "hard line vs. de-escalation." The base text leans toward condemnation, protection and a diplomatic break; the tabled amendments would graft on a call to avoid military escalation and a solidarity point that explicitly names international sanctions and geopolitical tensions among the population's burdens — a softer, sanctions-sceptical framing. The vote is partly about how punitive vs. how dialogue-first the message should be.
- **Second-order tension:** the proposers' own "break all diplomatic normalisation … by all financial means" sits in tension with the amendment-line worry that sanctions add suffering to suffering — the same humanitarian concern pulls in opposite operational directions.
- **Read on motive:** broad cross-party sponsorship signals a consensus-symbolism play; the contested amendments are where genuine values divergence (interventionist condemnation vs. anti-sanction caution) surfaces.
proposed_by: PS, DéFI, Ecolo, Team Fouad Ahidar (Aït Baala, Ghyssels, Ikazban, Maison, Khattabi, Ahidar)

headline: Grant the newly sworn-in Brussels regional government Parliament's confidence so it can take office and govern for the rest of the term.
title: L'ordre du jour appelle le vote nominatif sur la motion de confiance déposée par le gouvernement à l'issue de sa déclaration. Après plus de six cents jours, les Bruxellois ont enfin un gouvernement. Quelqu'un demande-t-il la parole pour une explication de vote ?
raw_outcome: L'ordre du jour appelle le vote nominatif sur la motion de confiance déposée par le gouvernement à l'issue de sa déclaration. Après plus de six cents jours, les Bruxellois ont enfin un gouvernement. Quelqu'un demande-t-il la parole pour une explication de vote ?
source_brief:
After what the chair counted as more than 600 days — 614 by some tallies — without a formed government since the June 2024 election, a coalition finally took the oath before the King and is now asking Parliament to confirm it in office. The motion is the formal trigger: backing it installs this team for the roughly three years left in the term; withholding leaves Brussels without a full-powers executive.

- **What a yes actually does** — invests *this* government and ends the longest formation deadlock in the Region's history, letting it leave the provisional-twelfths budget regime behind.
- **The 24-page declaration** — the policy text runs 24 pages including the cover, and the GGC/Cocom budget is not slated for a vote for another three months, so confidence is granted before the spending plan is seen.
- **A heavy ledger comes with it** — a hiring freeze, lower discretionary subsidies for associations, no STIB fleet renewal, tighter housing investment, and higher water and STIB tariffs plus a planned car vignette.
- **The rub:** do you hand a government a vote of confidence on a thin, still-unbudgeted declaration just to end the paralysis — or refuse to write what critics call a blank cheque after 600 days of crisis?
deep_facts:
- The vote applies article 120 of Parliament's rules; the declaration was read on Monday 23 February 2026 and the confidence vote held Friday 27 February 2026 (CRI n°19, p.6).
- The chair stated Brussels had been without a formed government for 'more than six hundred days — six hundred and fourteen by some counters' since the June 2024 election (CRI n°19, p.6).
- The government was legally constituted before the vote: oath taken before the King, portfolios distributed, ministers and state secretaries appointed (Verstraeten, N-VA, p.10).
- The policy declaration runs 24 pages including the cover (de Patoul, DéFI, p.9; De Brabandere, Vlaams Belang, p.10).
- The Cocom/GGC budget is to be submitted to a vote only in roughly three months (Khattabi, Ecolo, p.6).
- Measures cited from the declaration: a moratorium on public-sector hiring; reduced facultative (discretionary) subsidies for associations; status quo on STIB service with ageing rolling stock not replaced; disinvestment in public housing; tariff rises including water and STIB; a planned car vignette (De Smedt, PTB, pp.8-9).
- PTB framed it as 'one billion less' in the regional budget — '80% cuts and 20% drawn from workers' pockets' (PTB, p.9).
- Following the vote the chair fixed the attributions and naming of eight permanent commissions under article 23.1 (CRI n°19, p.11): Environment; Spatial Planning; Finance and General Affairs; Housing; Internal Affairs; Mobility; Economic Affairs; Equal Opportunities and Women's Rights.
- Several opposition speakers (DéFI, N-VA, Vlaams Belang) criticised the absence of an electoral-system reform from the declaration, citing it as a cause of the 614-day blockage (de Patoul, p.9).
deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- Investiture votes are near-formalities once a coalition is sworn in; the real content here is the speeches, which preview the term's battle lines (austerity, Good Move/mobility, the unvoted GGC budget) rather than the office question itself.
- Sequencing the vote *before* the GGC budget — three months out — front-loads the political risk onto critics: a yes endorses spending nobody has yet seen, which is precisely the 'blank cheque' charge being lodged.
- The opposition's repeated framing — 'what are we even voting on?', 'a government on paper' — is an attempt to delegitimise the mandate rather than contest a policy, a posture that costs little and positions them for 2029.
- Pairing the vote with the immediate re-fixing of eight commissions signals the machinery is being restarted at speed after the provisional-twelfths limbo.
proposed_by: The Brussels regional government (minister-president Boris Dilliès), tabled at the close of its policy declaration of 23 February 2026; majority of PS, MR, Open VLD/Anders., Les Engagés, Groen, cd&v and Vooruit.brussels.

headline: Call for an immediate and permanent ceasefire in Darfur and Sudan and for strengthening and securing humanitarian aid and arms-transfer controls in the conflict.
title: Notre proposition de résolution appelle à un cessez-le-feu immédiat et permanent. Elle exige un accès humanitaire sûr et sans entraves, soutient la lutte contre l'impunité et rappelle la nécessité d'un contrôle strict des transferts d'armes, afin que nos politiques économiques ne puissent alimenter directement ou indirectement les logiques miliciennes.
raw_outcome: Notre proposition de résolution appelle à un cessez-le-feu immédiat et permanent. Elle exige un accès humanitaire sûr et sans entraves, soutient la lutte contre l'impunité et rappelle la nécessité d'un contrôle strict des transferts d'armes, afin que nos politiques économiques ne puissent alimenter directement ou indirectement les logiques miliciennes.
source_brief:
Brussels has no formal power over foreign policy, so this resolution is a political statement: it asks the Region to put its voice — as a host of the EU capital — behind an immediate, permanent ceasefire in the Sudan war and to press for safe, unobstructed humanitarian access. The text also calls for tight control of arms transfers and says the Region's own economic policy must not, directly or indirectly, feed the militias.

- **What it commits to** — a ceasefire demand, secured humanitarian corridors, support for international-justice mechanisms, and a call on the federal foreign minister to act.
- **The scale invoked** — speakers cite up to ~25 million people facing hunger, ~21 million in acute food insecurity, civilian deaths more than doubling in 2025, and ~75% of health facilities no longer functioning.
- **The Region's one real lever** — arms-export licensing: speakers argue Brussels must block any weapon exports usable to commit war crimes, and extend the embargo now limited to Darfur.
- **The rub:** does a regional parliament with no foreign-affairs competence add weight by speaking out — or is a symbolic text that 'won't end the war' a distraction, especially when some argue it stays silent on European and Belgian responsibility for the crisis?
deep_facts:
- The conflict is dated to April 2023, opposing the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF); described as one of the world's gravest humanitarian crises (Diallo, Les Engagés, p.15).
- Figures cited in debate: nearly 25 million people suffering hunger and nearly 75% of health structures no longer functioning (Ahidar, p.19); about 21 million people in acute food insecurity (Maison, DéFI, p.20); 15 million children needing urgent humanitarian aid (Parga Vega, PTB, p.23); civilian deaths reported to have more than doubled during 2025, per the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights before the Human Rights Council in Geneva (Maison, p.20).
- Documented violence cited: Al-Geneïna and El-Facher/Al-Fashir besieged, bombed and starved; hospitals destroyed; sexual violence used as a weapon of terror (against women and girls, and noted also against boys and men by Groothedde, Groen, p.22); drone strikes on vital infrastructure intensifying since the start of 2026 (Maison, p.20).
- Belgian/federal actions referenced: foreign minister Maxime Prévot announced in August 2025 a release of €5 million to the UN Humanitarian Fund for Sudan, Belgium's first contribution to that fund; a Belgian contribution of US$20 million to the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF); Belgium co-signed on 18-19 February 2026 a joint declaration condemning attacks on civilians and hospitals in Kordofan and Darfur (Diallo, pp.15-16).
- Operative asks of the text: immediate and permanent ceasefire; safe, unobstructed humanitarian access; support for international-justice mechanisms and the fight against impunity; strict control of arms transfers; and that the Region's economic policy not arm the militias (Diallo, p.15).
- The arms-export point invokes Amnesty International secretary-general Agnès Callamard urging expansion of the Darfur arms embargo to the rest of the country; the Region holds competence over arms trade (Groothedde, Groen, pp.22-23).
- The text was adopted unanimously in committee beforehand; it emerged from a cross-group working group that integrated amendments from nearly all groups (Ikazban, PS, p.16-17).
- PTB/PVDA stated reservations that the text is superficial on the deep causes and on European and Belgian responsibility (citing the 2014 Khartoum Process and a 2017 collaboration with the al-Bashir regime to return refugees), while indicating support out of solidarity (Parga Vega, PTB, pp.23-24).
deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- The Region candidly lacks foreign-policy competence, so the resolution's real function is reputational and signalling — speakers explicitly tie it to 'restoring Brussels' image' and to consistency with prior texts on Iran and Gaza.
- The single binding lever is arms-export licensing, a genuine regional competence; the rest is an appeal to the federal minister, which makes the text strong on symbolism and weak on enforcement.
- Building it through a cross-party working group with near-unanimous amendments is designed to maximise moral weight and pre-empt the 'why is a regional parliament doing foreign policy?' objection raised by N-VA-adjacent critics.
- The PTB/PVDA stance — backing the text while attacking it for ignoring European/Belgian culpability — lets them claim solidarity without endorsing what they read as a sanitised account of the war's causes.
proposed_by: Elhadj Moussa Diallo (Les Engagés, lead author), Jamal Ikazban (PS), Benjamin Dalle (cd&v), Gladys Kazadi, Alain Deneef (Les Engagés), Mounir Laarissi, Fouad Ahidar, Gisèle Mandaila; later co-signed by Zakia Khattabi (Ecolo). Resolution A-215.

headline: Give assent to an interregional cooperation agreement making producers of packaging, tobacco, wipes and similar products fund the waste-management and street-cleaning costs their products create.
title: Le projet d'ordonnance concrétise le principe du pollueur-payeur : les producteurs d'emballages, de produits de tabac, de lingettes, etc., devront assumer le financement de la gestion des déchets issus de leurs produits ainsi que les coûts liés à la propreté publique. Cet accord permettra à la Région de percevoir des recettes estimées à 50 millions d'euros par an, dont 54 % alloués aux communes pour le volet des déchets sauvages.
raw_outcome: Le projet d'ordonnance concrétise le principe du pollueur-payeur : les producteurs d'emballages, de produits de tabac, de lingettes, etc., devront assumer le financement de la gestion des déchets issus de leurs produits ainsi que les coûts liés à la propreté publique. Cet accord permettra à la Région de percevoir des recettes estimées à 50 millions d'euros par an, dont 54 % alloués aux communes pour le volet des déchets sauvages.
source_brief:
Today, when a discarded cigarette butt, wipe or food wrapper is cleaned off a Brussels street, the public pays. This agreement flips that under the polluter-pays principle: makers of packaging, tobacco, wipes, balloons, chewing gum and textiles would have to reimburse the cost of managing their products' waste and of keeping public space clean — money the Region estimates at about €50 million a year, with 54% of the litter share going to the 19 municipalities and 46% kept by the Region.

- **Why now** — it transposes the EU Single-Use Plastics (SUP) directive; speakers warned that not adopting it risks EU financial penalties and loses another year of revenue.
- **The model chosen** — a 'financial' model: producers reimburse public bodies rather than run the cleaning themselves, which proponents say rules out privatising street-cleaning.
- **The long delay's price tag** — one speaker estimated Belgium's institutional slowness let industry save roughly €465 million at the public's expense; new revenue is earmarked for the regional waste prevention/sorting/recycling fund.
- **The rub:** does forcing producers to pay finally relieve municipal budgets and your local taxes — or, as sceptics warn, will firms simply pass the new charge on to households and small shops while big online platforms slip through?
deep_facts:
- The text gives assent to the interregional cooperation agreement of 9 February 2026 on Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR/REP) for certain waste streams and litter ('déchets sauvages'), and amends the ordinance of 12 December 1991 creating budgetary funds (CRI n°21, p.18; A-264).
- It is the outcome of five years of negotiation between the federated entities; presented by secretary of state Ans Persoons (rapporteur Laarissi, p.19).
- Estimated new revenue for the Region: ~€50 million per year (rapporteur, p.19).
- Litter-share split: 54% to the municipalities, 46% to the Region (rapporteur, pp.18-19); the exact inter-municipal distribution key is to be set by a government decree still in preparation (Persoons, p.20).
- Mechanism: a 'financial' model — producers reimburse costs borne by public bodies, which proponents say avoids privatising public cleaning (rapporteur, p.19).
- Revenue is assigned to the Fund for the prevention, sorting, reuse, recycling and valorisation of waste, which already collects the incineration-tax receipts (rapporteur, p.20).
- Producers covered include packaging, tobacco products, wipes, balloons, chewing gum and the textile sector (rapporteur/de Patoul, pp.18-21).
- Chewing gum is not covered by the EU SUP directive, so a flat-rate ('forfaitaire') contribution was decided for it, with a budget of €3.5 million cited and an evaluation within two years (de Patoul / Persoons, pp.20-21).
- Cost comparison cited: clearing illegal dumping/litter costs ~€51 million in Brussels versus ~€71 million in Flanders — about four times more per inhabitant, attributed by the state secretary to population density and tourist influx (Vanden Borre, N-VA / Persoons, pp.20-21).
- DéFI estimated Belgium's institutional slowness let industry save ~€465 million at the collectivity's expense (de Patoul, p.21).
- Driver: transposition of the EU Single-Use Plastics (SUP) directive; the text was treated as urgent to avoid EU financial penalties for SUP infringements and to avoid losing another year of revenue (rapporteur, p.19).
- Online commerce: foreign platforms are to be made responsible via a mandatary ('mandataire') system, obliging them to assume EPR if their sellers do not (Persoons, p.20).
- A deposit-return scheme ('consigne'/statiegeld) on cans is neither imposed nor excluded; the coalition agreement provides for working on it during the term (Persoons, pp.20-21).
- Committee vote stages (procedural): article 1 carried 14 votes with 1 abstention; articles 2 and 3 each 10 votes with 4 abstentions; the whole project 10 for with 4 abstentions (rapporteur, p.21).
deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- The 'financial' model (producers reimburse, public bodies keep doing the cleaning) is the politically safest design: it captures the money while neutralising the privatisation fear that an operational-EPR model would trigger from unions and the left.
- The €465 million 'savings' figure reframes five years of institutional delay as a direct transfer from the public purse to industry — a useful frame for proponents to argue urgency and for critics to attack Belgium's federal complexity.
- The unresolved inter-municipal distribution key (left to a future decree) is where the real money fight will play out: 54% sounds settled, but who among the 19 communes gets what is not, so the headline split can still be hollowed in implementation.
- The deposit-return scheme being explicitly left open is a deliberate fudge papering over a real majority split (Groen/Ecolo pro-consigne, MR wary of disrupting the blue-bag chain), deferred to avoid blocking the broader text.
- The cost-pass-through worry (households/small shops paying instead of polluters) is the genuine equity hinge: whether EPR bites producers or just relabels a consumer charge depends on enforcement detail the ordinance does not itself guarantee.
proposed_by: Brussels regional government project of ordinance (A-264), defended in the Environment commission by secretary of state Ans Persoons; assent to the interregional cooperation agreement of 9 February 2026.

headline: Adopt the Brussels-Capital Region's 2026 revenue budget ("voies et moyens"), fixing forecast receipts and the year's borrowing authorisations to fund regional spending.
title: Projet d'ordonnance contenant le budget des voies et moyens de la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale pour l'année budgétaire 2026. Après les douzièmes provisoires, la Région se dote enfin d'un véritable budget initial, fixant le solde SEC à moins de 957 millions d'euros et amorçant une trajectoire de retour à l'équilibre à l'horizon 2029.
raw_outcome: Projet d'ordonnance contenant le budget des voies et moyens de la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale pour l'année budgétaire 2026. Après les douzièmes provisoires, la Région se dote enfin d'un véritable budget initial, fixant le solde SEC à moins de 957 millions d'euros et amorçant une trajectoire de retour à l'équilibre à l'horizon 2029.
source_brief:
This is the income side of the Region's budget for 2026 — the receipts it expects to collect and the borrowing it is authorised to take on. It matters because, for the first time in over a year, the Region is setting a full initial budget rather than improvising.

- **First real budget in 615 days.** Brussels had been running on five successive sets of provisional "twelfths" — monthly stopgaps that kept the lights on but rolled deficits forward with no clear plan.
- **A deep hole to fill.** The Region starts from a structural deficit cited in debate at around 1.5 billion euros, with a stated goal of reaching balance by 2029.
- **Heavy reliance on borrowing.** Interest on the existing debt alone is set to cost about 500 million euros in 2026; the revenue side has to be read against that load.
- **The rub:** balancing the books means either raising more revenue or borrowing more — and critics argue the receipts here are optimistic and the real adjustment is being pushed onto future years.
deep_facts:
- The text is the "projet d'ordonnance contenant le budget des voies et moyens de la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale pour l'année budgétaire 2026" (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- It follows a period in which the Region operated on provisional twelfths; the budget minister referred to "615 jours" and "cinq budgets provisoires successifs" before this initial budget (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- The 2026 budget fixes the SEC/ESR balance at under -957 million euros ("le solde SEC à moins de 957 millions d'euros"), with a stated trajectory back to balance by 2029 (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- The minister stated the budget improves by 591 million euros versus the previous year, citing the Court of Auditors (Cour des comptes), equal to about 9% of revenues (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- Interest on the debt is forecast at around 500 million euros in 2026; a 1-percentage-point rise in rates would add about 150 million euros (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- A debt ceiling of 3 billion euros was set; direct debt is estimated at 14.6 billion euros in 2026, rising to 15.6 (2027), 16.2 (2028) and 16.4 billion euros in 2029 (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- Regional debt was cited as having risen from 6 billion euros in 2019 to about 15 billion euros (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- Opposition members put the underlying deficit and off-budget operations differently, citing 400 million euros for the regional housing company (SLRB), 180 million for Vivaqua and 60 million for Kanal-Centre Pompidou, and a projected cumulative debt of 19.1 billion euros by 2029 (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- The revenue budget is the lever that lets the Region keep borrowing: voting it sets how much new debt the executive can legally raise this year.
- The fight is less about the numbers on the page than about whether the receipts are realistic — if they are over-stated, the gap re-appears as deeper borrowing later.
- Keeping large operations (housing, water, Kanal) off-budget flatters the headline balance, which is precisely the transparency point the Court of Auditors keeps flagging.

headline: Adopt the Brussels-Capital Region's 2026 general expenditure budget ("budget des dépenses"), authorising the year's spending and running a budget deficit.
title: Projet d'ordonnance contenant le budget général des dépenses de la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale pour l'année budgétaire 2026. Les primes du régime des agents contractuels subventionnés vont être réduites, Activa va être supprimé, les moyens financiers dédiés à l'emploi vont être diminués.
raw_outcome: Projet d'ordonnance contenant le budget général des dépenses de la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale pour l'année budgétaire 2026. Les primes du régime des agents contractuels subventionnés vont être réduites, Activa va être supprimé, les moyens financiers dédiés à l'emploi vont être diminués.
source_brief:
This is the spending side of the Region's 2026 budget — the credits each policy area is authorised to spend. Paired with the revenue text, it is the Region's first full initial budget after a long run on provisional twelfths.

- **It sets the deficit.** The 2026 budget is planned to close in the red, with the SEC/ESR balance fixed at under -957 million euros.
- **From stopgap to plan.** For more than a year the Region spent through monthly provisional twelfths, which guaranteed continuity of public services but rolled deficits forward without a clear direction.
- **Savings land on real programmes.** Debate flagged cuts touching employment measures — reduced subsidised-contract premiums and the end of the Activa scheme among them.
- **The rub:** the only ways to shrink a 1.5-billion-euro deficit are to cut spending or raise revenue — and where the axe falls (employment, social programmes) is exactly what the budget is fought over.
deep_facts:
- The text is the "projet d'ordonnance contenant le budget général des dépenses de la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale pour l'année budgétaire 2026" (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- It is the companion expenditure text to the 2026 revenue budget, the Region having previously operated on provisional twelfths (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- The 2026 budget fixes the SEC/ESR balance at under -957 million euros, with a stated return to balance targeted for 2029, from a deficit cited at about 1.5 billion euros (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- The minister stated the budget improves by 591 million euros versus the prior year, per the Court of Auditors, about 9% of revenues (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- Debate cited spending cuts in employment policy: reduced premiums for subsidised contractual agents (ACS), suppression of the Activa scheme, and a lower employment budget; one figure given was 16,500 insertion pathways concerned (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- Several amendments were tabled to the expenditure budget, including ones touching the totals of Bruxelles Environnement and STIB programmes (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- Investment in housing in 2026 was cited at around 150 million euros (compared to the debt-interest charge of about 500 million euros) (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- The expenditure budget is where the abstract "reduce the deficit" becomes concrete: every credit line cut is a programme that shrinks, which is why employment measures dominated the debate.
- Pairing a -957-million-euro planned deficit with a 2029 balance target signals front-loaded ambition — the political risk is that the cuts needed to hit that path arrive faster than the affected sectors can absorb.
- Reading this text against the revenue text shows the real choice: the same gap can be closed by spending less here or by borrowing/taxing more there.

headline: Enact the formal regulation carrying the 2026 revenue budget of the Brussels Agglomeration, the companion text to the Region's own revenue budget.
title: Projet de règlement contenant le budget des voies et moyens de l'Agglomération de Bruxelles pour l'année budgétaire 2026.
raw_outcome: Projet de règlement contenant le budget des voies et moyens de l'Agglomération de Bruxelles pour l'année budgétaire 2026.
source_brief:
This is the formal regulation ("règlement") setting the 2026 revenue budget of the Brussels Agglomeration, the small legacy entity whose budget travels alongside the Region's. It carries the same 2026 context, the Region having spent over a year on provisional twelfths.

- **A procedural twin.** It mirrors the main revenue budget for the Agglomeration's separate accounts.
- **The rub:** it is technical, but voting it through is part of finally closing the door on budgeting by monthly stopgap.
deep_facts:
- The text is the "projet de règlement contenant le budget des voies et moyens de l'Agglomération de Bruxelles pour l'année budgétaire 2026" (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- It is the Agglomeration's revenue companion to the Region's 2026 voies-et-moyens budget; the regulation is submitted for sanction by the government (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- It shares the same 2026 initial-budget context that followed the period of provisional twelfths (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- This is a near-mechanical companion vote: the Agglomeration's accounts must move in lockstep with the Region's, so the substantive choices sit in the main revenue budget, not here.

title: Projet de règlement contenant le budget général des dépenses de l'Agglomération de Bruxelles pour l'année budgétaire 2026.
raw_outcome: Projet de règlement contenant le budget général des dépenses de l'Agglomération de Bruxelles pour l'année budgétaire 2026.
source_brief:
This is the formal regulation ("règlement") setting the 2026 expenditure budget of the Brussels Agglomeration, the legacy entity whose accounts run alongside the Region's. It carries the same 2026 context, after a long stretch of provisional twelfths.

- **A procedural twin.** It mirrors the main expenditure budget for the Agglomeration's separate accounts.
- **The rub:** procedural, but it completes the set of texts that replace budgeting by monthly stopgap with a full 2026 budget.
deep_facts:
- The text is the "projet de règlement contenant le budget général des dépenses de l'Agglomération de Bruxelles pour l'année budgétaire 2026" (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- It is the Agglomeration's expenditure companion to the Region's 2026 expenditure budget; the regulation is submitted for sanction by the government (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).

headline: Amend the pension rules for former Brussels MPs to let their pensions be indexed again, lifting the freeze that follows from the federal salary-indexation pause.
title: Proposition de décision visant à permettre l'indexation des pensions des anciens députés bruxellois. Comme le montant de ces pensions est calculé sur la base du salaire des députés de la Chambre des représentants, et que le niveau fédéral a décidé de ne plus indexer ces salaires jusqu'en 2029, les pensions des députés bruxellois à la retraite sont automatiquement bloquées, sauf si une décision permet le contraire.
raw_outcome: Proposition de décision visant à permettre l'indexation des pensions des anciens députés bruxellois. Comme le montant de ces pensions est calculé sur la base du salaire des députés de la Chambre des représentants, et que le niveau fédéral a décidé de ne plus indexer ces salaires jusqu'en 2029, les pensions des députés bruxellois à la retraite sont automatiquement bloquées, sauf si une décision permet le contraire.
source_brief:
This changes the rules on pensions paid to former members of the Brussels Parliament so they can be indexed — raised in line with the cost of living — again. The catch is a chain reaction from the federal level.

- **Why they are frozen.** These pensions are calculated on the salary of federal Chamber MPs. The federal level decided not to index those salaries until 2029, so the Brussels pensions are automatically blocked unless a separate decision says otherwise.
- **What it does.** It creates the legal basis to index the pensions despite that federal freeze, with an amendment making it take effect from 1 March 2026.
- **The numbers in play.** Debate cited an average former-MP pension of about 2,000 euros a month, with older mandates reaching far higher.
- **The rub:** indexing protects retirees against inflation — but applied here it lifts pensions already described as several times the average, raising the fairness question of who gets shielded from a freeze that hits everyone else.
deep_facts:
- The text is a "proposition de décision visant à modifier le règlement fixant le régime des pensions attribuées aux anciens membres du Parlement de la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale en vue de l'indexation des pensions" (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- Former Brussels MPs' pensions are calculated on the salary of federal Chamber of Representatives MPs; the federal level decided not to index those salaries until 2029, which automatically freezes the Brussels pensions "sauf si une décision permet le contraire" (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- An amendment by two members gives the change retroactive effect from 1 March 2026 ("L'article 1er produit ses effets le 1er mars 2026"), with the pension fund (Caisse de retraite) to execute it without delay (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- Debate cited the average former-MP pension at about 2,000 euros per month, corresponding to nine years of parliamentary mandate (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- For a five-year mandate after 2019, the pension was cited at roughly 800 euros gross per month; for earlier mandates it could reach about 7,800 euros gross per month (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- The Wijninckx ceiling was cited at 8,329 euros gross per month; debate noted past cases of MPs receiving up to 20% above it, since ended, and that fourteen former Brussels MPs who litigated to exceed the ceiling were all dismissed (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
- For comparison, Statbel figures cited put the 2025 average pension at 2,252 euros for men and 1,853 euros gross for women (CRI, 27 Mar 2026).
deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- The mechanism is the real story: by pegging its pensions to a federal salary the Region cannot control, Brussels imported a freeze it never voted for — this text is the manual override.
- Framing it as "indexation" makes it sound like routine inflation protection, but applied to pensions cited at multiples of the national average it is politically a top-up, which is the wedge the opposition presses.
- The 1 March 2026 retroactivity means the override is designed to bridge the freeze seamlessly, leaving no gap month — a sign the drafters wanted continuity, not a one-off catch-up.

headline: Update the legal definition of a "distributed-ledger address" (a blockchain/crypto wallet address) in Brussels tax law, so the Region's reporting rules track the EU framework for taxing crypto-assets.
title: Projet d'ordonnance modifiant la définition de l'adresse de registre distribué dans l'article 5, 31°, de l'ordonnance du 26 juillet 2013 transposant la directive 2011/16/UE du Conseil du 15 février 2011 relative à la coopération administrative dans le domaine fiscal et abrogeant la directive 77/799/CEE. M. Gilles Verstraeten, rapporteur, se réfère au rapport écrit.
raw_outcome: Projet d'ordonnance modifiant la définition de l'adresse de registre distribué dans l'article 5, 31°, de l'ordonnance du 26 juillet 2013 transposant la directive 2011/16/UE du Conseil du 15 février 2011 relative à la coopération administrative dans le domaine fiscal et abrogeant la directive 77/799/CEE. M. Gilles Verstraeten, rapporteur, se réfère au rapport écrit.
source_brief:
This is a narrow, technical fix to Brussels tax law: it rewrites the definition of an "adresse de registre distribué" — in plain terms, a blockchain or crypto wallet address — inside article 5, 31° of the 26 July 2013 ordinance that transposed EU Directive 2011/16/UE on administrative cooperation between tax authorities. The point is to keep the Region's crypto-asset reporting rules aligned with the EU's tax framework, so that holdings and transfers tied to wallet addresses can be reported and exchanged between tax administrations.

- **What it actually changes:** one definition in an existing 2013 ordinance — not blockchain regulation in general, just the term the tax-reporting rules hang on.
- **Why now:** it brings Brussels into line with the EU's expanding cooperation framework for taxing crypto-assets, where wallet addresses are the hook for identifying who owes what.
- **Who it touches:** people and platforms holding or moving crypto-assets, whose wallet data feeds cross-border tax-information exchange.
- **The rub:** is keeping tax authorities able to trace crypto wallets a sensible plug of an avoidance gap, or an extension of fiscal surveillance into a space people expected to stay private? Voting for adopts the update; voting against leaves the older definition in place.
deep_facts:
- The text is a projet d'ordonnance modifying the definition of "adresse de registre distribué" (distributed-ledger / blockchain address) in article 5, 31° of the ordinance of 26 July 2013 (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
- That 2013 ordinance transposed Council Directive 2011/16/UE of 15 February 2011 on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation, repealing Directive 77/799/CEE (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
- The amendment concerns the definition used for tax-reporting/cooperation purposes; it does not regulate blockchain technology generally (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
- In the plenary, the rapporteur (M. Gilles Verstraeten) referred to the written report; the general discussion was opened and closed without floor debate (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
- Articles 1, then 2 to 3, were examined without observation in the article-by-article discussion ahead of the nominal vote on the whole (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
- Reference numbers: A-274/1, 2 et 3 – 2025/2026 (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- The change reads as a DAC8-type alignment: the EU has been extending Directive 2011/16/UE to cover crypto-assets, and a stale wallet-address definition would leave Brussels' reporting rules out of step with that exchange of tax information.
- The absence of floor debate signals this was treated as a consensual technical transposition rather than a contested policy choice — the substantive arguments (crypto avoidance vs. fiscal privacy) sit at the EU level, not in this single-definition tweak.
- For a citizen, the live question is less about this clause than about the direction it serves: tighter traceability of crypto holdings for tax purposes.

headline: Decline to raise a conflict-of-interest objection against federal bill 56-1342, letting the federal reform that merges Brussels' six local police zones into one proceed without the Region forcing a formal pause for inter-parliamentary talks.
title: Conclusions de la commission tendant au rejet de la proposition de motion relative à un conflit d'intérêts avec la Chambre des représentants concernant le projet de loi n° 56-1342 modifiant la loi du 7 décembre 1998 organisant un service de police intégré structuré à deux niveaux. Quelle que soit votre position à propos de la fusion des zones de police, si vous voulez faire en sorte que Bruxelles soit entendue, il faut voter en faveur de cette motion.
raw_outcome: Conclusions de la commission tendant au rejet de la proposition de motion relative à un conflit d'intérêts avec la Chambre des représentants concernant le projet de loi n° 56-1342 modifiant la loi du 7 décembre 1998 organisant un service de police intégré structuré à deux niveaux. Quelle que soit votre position à propos de la fusion des zones de police, si vous voulez faire en sorte que Bruxelles soit entendue, il faut voter en faveur de cette motion.
source_brief:
Federal bill 56-1342 would merge Brussels' six local police zones into a single zone. A conflict-of-interest motion was tabled to force a formal pause and oblige the federal and regional parliaments to talk before the bill is finalised — a procedural lever, not an outright veto, meant to make Brussels' voice heard on a reform that reshapes how its policing is organised. What is on the table now is the committee's recommendation to **not pursue** that objection.

- **What you are voting on:** the committee's conclusion to set the conflict-of-interest motion aside. Voting **for** = decline to raise the objection and let the federal police-zone reform run its course. Voting **against** = pursue the objection and trigger the inter-parliamentary pause.
- **The case to pursue it:** supporters argue no Brussels security actor — the 19 mayors, the public prosecutor, the chief commissioners, the police unions — backs the forced merger, that Brussels police are underfunded by an estimated 80 million euros a year, and that the Region is being reshaped without a say.
- **The case to let it proceed:** others point to Brussels' security record — 62 shootings in 2023, 92 in 2024, 101 in 2025, and 19% of residents feeling often or always unsafe — and treat the merger as an overdue, necessary response.
- **The rub:** should Brussels spend its institutional lever to stall a federal security reform it had little hand in, or step aside and let it happen? The direction matters — a "for" here clears the merger's path; an "against" puts it on hold.
deep_facts:
- The item is the committee's "conclusions tendant au rejet" of the proposition de motion relative to a conflict of interest with the Chamber of Representatives concerning federal bill n° 56-1342 (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
- Bill 56-1342 modifies the law of 7 December 1998 organising an integrated, two-level police service and the law of 26 April 2002 on essential elements of the status of police-service personnel; it provides for merging Brussels' six local police zones into one (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
- The conflict-of-interest mechanism is described as an institutional tool to make institutional loyalty function: when one entity of the federal state takes a decision affecting another, the latter may request to be heard and to open discussion between parliaments — a pause, not a veto (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
- Proponents stated that all 19 Brussels mayors had criticised the merger, including some now in government (Henry, Laaouej, Dilliès), and that the public prosecutor (M. Moinil), chief commissioners and police unions did not advocate for it (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
- Figures cited for underfunding: federal dotation of about 37,000 euros per year per Brussels officer versus 50,000 euros per federal officer (KUL norm); Bruxelles Pouvoirs locaux estimated the shortfall at about 80 million euros per year (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
- Federal minister Quintin was cited as proposing 55 million euros over five years (about 11 million per year) for the police reform, characterised by proponents as insufficient against an 80-million-per-year structural deficit (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
- The KUL norm dates from 2002, based on 1999 population figures; proponents noted Brussels' population had since grown by roughly 25% without a corresponding revision (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
- Arguments for the merger cited the Flemish Peace Institute ranking Brussels among Europe's top three cities for gang violence and shootings, alongside Naples and Marseille; shootings reported as 62 in 2023, 92 in 2024 and 101 in 2025; 19% of residents feeling often or always unsafe in their neighbourhood, 42% fearing aggression, 30% theft (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
- The federal bill on the merger was reported as adopted in federal committee less than two days before this sitting, with no accompanying text on a KUL-norm reform (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
- Reference numbers: A-273/1, 2 et 3 – 2025/2026 (CRI, 24 Apr 2026).
deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- The framing as "conclusions tending to reject the motion" inverts the intuitive direction: a vote in favour does not endorse the conflict-of-interest objection — it endorses setting it aside, clearing the path for the federal merger. Voters who care about the substance must read past the procedural wrapper.
- The conflict-of-interest motion is as much about institutional leverage as about policing: proponents repeatedly framed it as a test of whether Brussels MPs answer to their region or to their (largely Walloon/Flemish-led) federal party lines.
- The funding figures (37k vs 50k per officer, an 80M/year gap, 55M over five years) are the proponents' core argument that a merger without refinancing changes the org chart but not the resourcing — while the security statistics (rising shootings, fear indicators) are the counter-frame for treating the merger as urgent.
- That the federal bill cleared committee two days earlier, without the promised KUL-norm reform, is the timing wedge proponents used to argue the pause is the Region's last realistic moment to be heard.
proposed_by: C. Jodogne, B. Clerfayt, J. Maison, J. De Patoul, Z. Khattabi, F. Maingain (DéFI / Ecolo)

headline: Vote to fast-track onto today's agenda a proposal opening a parliamentary commission of inquiry into how the Anderlecht public social-housing company is run.
title: « Je demande donc non seulement la prise en consideration en urgence de ce texte, mais aussi l'instauration en urgence de la commission d'enquete. Nous ne pouvons pas nous permettre d'attendre trois mois. » La demande porte sur l'instauration d'une commission d'enquete parlementaire concernant la gestion du Foyer anderlechtois (n° A-293/1 – 2025/2026), a la suite d'un reportage de l'emission « Pano ».
raw_outcome: « Je demande donc non seulement la prise en consideration en urgence de ce texte, mais aussi l'instauration en urgence de la commission d'enquete. Nous ne pouvons pas nous permettre d'attendre trois mois. » La demande porte sur l'instauration d'une commission d'enquete parlementaire concernant la gestion du Foyer anderlechtois (n° A-293/1 – 2025/2026), a la suite d'un reportage de l'emission « Pano ».
source_brief:
The request would suspend the normal timetable and put a proposal to open a parliamentary commission of inquiry into the management of the Foyer anderlechtois — a public social-housing company — straight onto today's agenda, rather than waiting for a committee meeting weeks away.

- **What triggered it:** a VRT *Pano* broadcast alleging "a system of abuse of power and clientelism" inside the company, including irregular allocation of social housing.
- **What an inquiry would do:** a parliamentary commission of inquiry has investigative powers to examine the facts; backers stress it is not in itself a verdict of guilt.
- **The clock:** if not fast-tracked, the text would go to the Finance and General Affairs Committee for its sitting on 1 June.
- **The rub:** whether grave allegations justify expediting an inquiry the same day, or whether the case is better served by the normal committee route a few days later — especially with a judicial investigation already open.
deep_facts:
- The text is proposal A-293/1 – 2025/2026, seeking a parliamentary commission of inquiry into the management of the Foyer anderlechtois, a public social-housing company (societe immobiliere de service public, SISP) (CRI, 22 May 2026).
- The request is to modify the order of the day to add the urgent taking-into-consideration AND immediate urgent debate of the text; absent urgency, it would be referred to the Finance and General Affairs Committee meeting of 1 June (CRI, 22 May 2026).
- The trigger cited is a VRT *Pano* report broadcast that week describing, per speakers, "clientelisme, interventionnisme, non-respect des regles et violation de la vie privee" and "un systeme d'abus et de clientelisme" at the Foyer anderlechtois (CRI, 22 May 2026).
- Speakers state a judicial investigation ("une enquete judiciaire") has already been opened into the matter (CRI, 22 May 2026).
- Some speakers additionally asked that the company's president and Anderlecht housing alderman, Lotfi Mostefa, be suspended from his functions while the inquiry runs; backers underline an inquiry does not equal a condemnation (CRI, 22 May 2026).
- Procedurally the president put the question of referral to the 1 June committee first; the proposers insisted on a vote on urgency instead, so the urgency was put to a vote of the 77 members present (CRI, 22 May 2026).
deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- Fast-tracking the same day is about control of the narrative as much as the calendar: a media scandal loses momentum within days, so backers want the inquiry visibly launched while attention is high.
- The parallel demand to suspend the company president folds a personnel sanction into a procedural urgency vote, raising the stakes well above scheduling.
- The 1 June committee date functions as the off-ramp: opposing urgency does not require opposing an inquiry, which lets reluctant members back the substance while resisting the rushed format.
- An open judicial probe gives sceptics a ready argument that a parliamentary inquiry the same day risks cutting across the courts.
proposed_by: Kalvin Soiresse Njall, Zakia Khattabi, Alain Maron, Joelle Maison (Ecolo)

headline: Vote to fast-track onto the agenda a conflict-of-interest motion against a French Community draft decree that would raise university tuition toward 1,250 euros, before that assembly votes next week.
title: « Je demande egalement l'urgence pour un deuxieme texte, qui consiste en une motion en conflit d'interets a la suite du debat en Federation Wallonie-Bruxelles sur l'augmentation du minerval a 1.250 euros (n° A-294/1 – 2025/2026). » L'urgence est invoquee parce que le vote en seance pleniere du Parlement de la Federation Wallonie-Bruxelles doit avoir lieu mercredi, le but etant d'evaluer l'impact sur les finances communales et les CPAS.
raw_outcome: « Je demande egalement l'urgence pour un deuxieme texte, qui consiste en une motion en conflit d'interets a la suite du debat en Federation Wallonie-Bruxelles sur l'augmentation du minerval a 1.250 euros (n° A-294/1 – 2025/2026). » L'urgence est invoquee parce que le vote en seance pleniere du Parlement de la Federation Wallonie-Bruxelles doit avoir lieu mercredi, le but etant d'evaluer l'impact sur les finances communales et les CPAS.
source_brief:
The request would put a conflict-of-interest motion straight onto the agenda now, so Brussels could act before the Federation Wallonie-Bruxelles (the French Community) holds its own plenary vote the following Wednesday.

- **The target:** a draft programme-decree of the French Community that includes raising the university registration fee (minerval) toward 1,250 euros.
- **The Brussels angle:** backers argue the measure would shift extra costs onto Brussels municipalities and their public welfare centres (CPAS), on top of other cost transfers.
- **Why now:** the French Community's plenary vote was due the following Wednesday, leaving a narrow window to register a conflict-of-interest objection.
- **The rub:** whether to drop this onto today's agenda to beat a neighbouring assembly's clock, or hold to the normal process even at the risk of missing that window.
deep_facts:
- The text is a conflict-of-interest motion, proposal A-294/1 – 2025/2026, concerning a debate in the Federation Wallonie-Bruxelles (French Community) on raising the minerval (university registration fee) "a 1.250 euros" (CRI, 22 May 2026).
- The stated ground for urgency is that the plenary vote in the French Community Parliament was due the following Wednesday; backers wanted time "d'evaluer l'impact de cette nouvelle mesure sur les finances communales, singulierement celles des CPAS" (CRI, 22 May 2026).
- Backers frame the measure as a potential "report de charges" (cost transfer) onto Brussels municipalities and CPAS, adding to transfers attributed to federal government decisions (CRI, 22 May 2026).
- In debate, figures cited for the fee impact varied by speaker: one stated current fees "entre 175 et 600 euros" rising "jusqu'a 1.200 euros"; the originating request referenced 1.250 euros (CRI, 22 May 2026).
- The request was to add the urgent taking-into-consideration of the text to the order of the day; absent urgency it would follow the normal procedure rather than being taken up the same day (CRI, 22 May 2026).
deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- A conflict-of-interest motion is a delaying lever: its value depends almost entirely on timing, so urgency is not a detail here but the whole point — miss the window and the instrument is spent.
- Framing a French-Community education measure as a Brussels budget problem (municipalities, CPAS) reroutes a debate the region cannot directly settle into one it can vote on.
- The differing fee figures (1.200 vs 1.250 euros) reflect the measure being mid-process in another assembly, so the exact number was still moving when urgency was sought.
- Voting against urgency need not mean endorsing the fee hike — it can simply reject using this assembly's agenda to intervene in another's pending vote.
